Utica.wildlife_intro:
Utica keeps our crew busy with Norway rats in the older mill neighborhoods, raccoons and squirrels in south-side attics, and bats in the big older homes. Mohawk River and Erie Canal  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Utica. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Utica jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Clinton.wildlife_intro:
Clinton is Oneida County's college village — Hamilton College on the hill, a groomed historic center around the village green, and streets of 1800s and early-1900s homes under deep canopy. Bats are Clinton's signature call, colonizing the eaves and attics of its historic housing, with squirrels a close second and raccoons in the village chimneys. Oriskany Creek winds through the valley below the college, feeding the insects the bats hunt.

Historic fabric rules the work in Clinton: original trim, slate and standing-seam roofs in places, and chimneys older than the village's incorporation. Our crew inspects Clinton homes with that fabric in view, removes the animals, and seals in ways that close gaps without scarring old work. Summer colonies here are frequently discovered during the college's quiet months, when village rentals and second homes sit still enough for bats to announce themselves.

Sherrill.wildlife_intro:
Sherrill is New York's smallest city — a tight community built around the Oneida silverware works, of modest, well-kept older homes on small lots, with Oneida Creek at its edge. Its calls are small-city calls: skunks under porches across the neighborhoods, opossums in the yards, squirrels in the older attics, and raccoons where the creek corridor meets the streets.

A city this compact has nowhere for a problem to hide for long — and no excuse for an incomplete job, either. Our crew inspects Sherrill homes completely, removes the animals, and screens the porch and shed voids that generate most of the city's complaints. The creek-side streets get foundation attention too, because Oneida Creek's banks deliver raccoons and skunks to the same few blocks nightly.
